channel.title: PsyDigest — psychiatry literature digest
channel.description: Summaries of new psychiatric research and guidelines

item.title: [35] The LAI-Oral Antipsychotic Efficacy-Effectiveness Paradox in Schizophrenia.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: The study examines why long-acting injectable (LAI) antipsychotics appear more effective in real-world observational studies than in randomized controlled trials (RCTs) for schizophrenia relapse prevention, a paradox that has persisted for decades and contributes to underuse of LAIs. The paper consists of a scoping review (PRISMA-ScR) and a conceptual methodological framework proposing solutions to resolve this paradox.
FINDINGS: The paradox is primarily attributed to confounding by indication in observational studies and inadequate adherence measurement across all designs. The authors propose four methodological solutions: (1) digital adherence monitoring (e.g., ingestible sensors), (2) pharmacogenomic stratification (e.g., CYP2D6, CYP3A4, CYP2C19 phenotyping), (3) pragmatic RCTs with real-world eligibility and objective adherence endpoints, and (4) AI-supported neuroimaging (PET/fMRI) to assess dopamine receptor occupancy and functional connectivity.
INTERPRETATION: The evidence is preliminary and conceptual rather than empirical, as the proposed solutions are not validated findings but a framework for future research. The scoping review highlights key methodological gaps (confounding, adherence measurement) but does not resolve the paradox. The proposed AI and neuroimaging approaches are innovative but require rigorous testing. The study underscores the need for better-designed comparative effectiveness research to guide clinical decisions.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Current evidence does not support a definitive superiority of LAIs over oral antipsychotics. Clinicians should remain cautious about overinterpreting observational findings favoring LAIs. Future research integrating digital monitoring, pharmacogenomics, and AI-driven neuroimaging may provide clearer guidance, but this is not yet actionable in routine practice.

item.title: [22] Efficacy of High-Frequency Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation Therapy for Depression With Insomnia Symptoms: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis Based on Randomized Controlled Trials.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This systematic review and meta-analysis assessed whether high-frequency repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (HF-rTMS) targeting the left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC) improves symptoms of depression and insomnia in patients with comorbid depression and insomnia, synthesizing 7 randomized controlled trials (RCTs) with 709 participants.
FINDINGS: HF-rTMS significantly improved sleep quality (SMD 0.97, 95% CI 0.23 to 1.71, p = 0.01) and depressive symptoms (SMD 0.61, 95% CI 0.38 to 0.84, p < 0.00001). Sleep latency showed a non-significant trend toward improvement (SMD 0.50, 95% CI -0.17 to 1.18, p = 0.14). Adverse events were not significantly different between groups (RR 1.09, 95% CI 0.80 to 1.48, p = 0.57). Substantial heterogeneity was present (I² = 91% for sleep quality), partly explained by differences in stimulation frequency and baseline antidepressant use.
INTERPRETATION: The evidence is of very-low to low certainty due to substantial heterogeneity, methodological limitations, and potential biases in included RCTs. While the pooled effects suggest benefit, the wide confidence intervals and inconsistency across studies limit confidence in the magnitude of effect. The lack of blinding in some trials and variability in protocols further reduce internal validity. Confirmation with larger, well-designed RCTs is needed before firm conclusions can be drawn.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Current evidence does not support routine use of HF-rTMS for comorbid depression and insomnia outside research settings. Clinicians should remain cautious and consider this modality only when standard treatments have failed, while awaiting higher-quality trials to clarify efficacy, optimal parameters, and patient selection.

item.title: [19] Is a ketogenic diet useful in the management of mood disorders?
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This narrative review examines whether a ketogenic diet (KD) can serve as an adjunctive treatment for mood disorders (MDs), summarizing recent randomized and prospective studies to assess efficacy and safety.
FINDINGS: The review reports that recent randomized and prospective studies suggest KD may improve depressive symptoms when used alongside standard treatments. However, potential adverse effects are noted, particularly in individuals with normal body weight or those without proper nutritional guidance. The lack of standardized KD protocols across studies complicates evidence synthesis.
INTERPRETATION: The evidence is preliminary and heterogeneous, with no clear consensus on KD implementation or outcomes. The review highlights the need for larger, well-powered randomized controlled trials (RCTs) with standardized protocols. Current findings are insufficient to support routine clinical use, and expert consensus on research protocols is a necessary next step before clinical guidelines can be developed.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: KD cannot yet be recommended for routine use in mood disorders. Clinicians should remain cautious, monitor emerging evidence, and avoid recommending KD without proper nutritional supervision due to potential risks.

item.title: [14] A digital platform for ADHD assessment and management: stakeholder-informed development and clinical implications.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: The study describes the development of a digital platform to operationalise the ADMiRE clinical pathway for ADHD assessment and management in Irish CAMHS, addressing variability in care despite established standards. The focus is on stakeholder-informed design to improve scalability and reduce administrative burden.
FINDINGS: The digital platform was developed through an iterative, stakeholder-informed process involving clinicians and service stakeholders. Key features include structured referral management, standardised diagnostic and monitoring tools with automated scoring, medication and case management, longitudinal monitoring, and automated clinical documentation. The system aims to support more consistent, guideline-informed care and reduce administrative burden while improving continuity across services.
INTERPRETATION: This is a perspective piece rather than a clinical study, so no effect sizes, confidence intervals, or p-values are reported. The strength lies in its stakeholder-informed, iterative development process, which enhances face validity and potential acceptability in routine CAMHS settings. However, as a perspective, it lacks empirical evaluation of clinical outcomes, cost-effectiveness, or implementation barriers. The generalisability to other healthcare systems or populations remains uncertain until further research is conducted.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: This digital platform may offer practical improvements in ADHD care by standardising assessment and management processes, but its clinical impact and feasibility in routine practice are unproven. Clinicians should await empirical validation before adopting this system.

item.title: [13] Anxiety and suicide risk: mechanism, timing, and clinical utility.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This narrative review examines whether anxiety symptoms or disorders add clinically useful information about suicide risk beyond what is captured by standard diagnoses or trait measures, and whether modifiable anxiety-related processes can inform prevention strategies.
FINDINGS: Across recent studies, panic disorder, generalized anxiety disorder, social anxiety disorder and PTSD show elevated suicide risk, but odds ratios attenuate after adjusting for depression and comorbidity. Within-person studies find that anxiety-related affect and rumination co-vary with suicidal thinking but rarely predict subsequent suicidal events. Several modifiable anxiety-related processes exist, yet durable reductions in suicidal outcomes have not been demonstrated.
INTERPRETATION: The evidence base is heterogeneous and largely observational, limiting causal inference. Adjustment for depression and comorbidity substantially reduces observed associations, suggesting anxiety alone is not a strong independent predictor. While modifiable processes exist, there is no proof that targeting them changes suicide risk; micro-randomized trials during acute risk periods are needed.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Current routine risk assessment should not rely on anxiety diagnoses or trait scales alone; instead, clinicians should monitor dynamic anxiety-related processes during high-risk periods, but should not expect such monitoring to reduce suicide risk until targeted interventions prove effective.

item.title: [13] Predicting olanzapine induced BMI increase using machine learning on population-based electronic health records.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: Weight gain is a frequent adverse effect of olanzapine, but predicting which patients will have clinically significant BMI increase is challenging in routine care. This retrospective cohort study used population-based Danish electronic health records (EHR) to develop and test machine-learning models that predict ≥5 % BMI increase after olanzapine initiation.
FINDINGS: The best-performing model (XGBoost) predicted ≥5 % BMI increase within 30–180 days after initiation with an AUROC of 0.72 (2016–2024 data) and 0.79 (held-out 2025 data). Prediction of on-treatment BMI increase to the next available follow-up yielded AUROC 0.71 (2016–2024) but dropped to 0.61 in 2025; standardising to 30–180 days lowered AUROC to 0.64 and 0.58. A minimal-feature model performed almost as well as the full model. Key predictors were lower baseline BMI, younger age, higher olanzapine dose, historical BMI variability and prior anxiolytic prescriptions.
INTERPRETATION: The moderate discrimination (AUROC ~0.72–0.79) suggests that EHR-based models can flag patients at higher risk of olanzapine-related weight gain, but performance declined in temporally external validation, indicating potential overfitting or dataset shift. The identified predictors align with known risk factors, lending face validity, yet the study is observational and cannot establish causality. External validation in other health systems and prospective evaluation of clinical utility are needed before any bedside implementation.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: These models may help clinicians identify patients who merit closer metabolic monitoring or early lifestyle interventions when olanzapine is started, but they should not replace clinical judgment or standard monitoring protocols until further validation is completed.

item.title: [11] Time for psychiatry to seriously consider broad-spectrum micronutrients.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: The article argues for considering broad-spectrum micronutrients (BSM) as a treatment option for psychological distress based on randomized controlled trials (RCTs) showing modest but positive effects on emotional regulation, irritability, and aggression. The clinical question is whether BSM should be integrated into psychiatric practice, and the population includes patients with psychological distress.
FINDINGS: The article cites RCTs where BSM demonstrated modest improvements in emotional regulation, irritability, and aggression, with effect sizes comparable to those seen with cognitive-behavioral therapy (CBT) and antidepressants. However, no specific numerical data (e.g., effect sizes, confidence intervals, p-values, or sample sizes) are provided in the abstract.
INTERPRETATION: The evidence presented is preliminary and lacks quantitative detail, making it difficult to assess the robustness of the findings. The claim that effect sizes are comparable to established treatments (CBT and antidepressants) is not substantiated with data in the abstract. The article does not address potential limitations such as heterogeneity in study populations, variability in micronutrient formulations, or long-term safety and efficacy. The argument for integrating BSM into practice is premature without more rigorous and detailed evidence.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: At present, this article does not provide sufficient evidence to change clinical practice. Further high-quality RCTs with detailed reporting of outcomes and safety data are needed before BSM can be considered a viable treatment option for psychological distress. Clinicians should remain cautious and rely on evidence-based treatments with well-established efficacy and safety profiles.

item.title: [11] Personality disorder and substance use disorder: an updated review.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This updated narrative review examines the comorbidity of personality disorder (PD) and substance use disorder (SUD), focusing on epidemiology, shared mechanisms, assessment, and management. It synthesizes recent evidence to inform clinical practice and research priorities.
FINDINGS: The review highlights a shift toward dimensional models (DSM-5 AMPD, ICD-11, HiTOP) and notes shared genetic, neurobiological, and environmental vulnerabilities (e.g., reward processing deficits, childhood adversity, negative affectivity, disinhibition). Digital phenotyping and machine learning are emerging tools for risk stratification. Integrated, personality-informed interventions show promise, with pharmacotherapy playing a supportive role. However, the authors emphasize the lack of robust longitudinal or interventional studies.
INTERPRETATION: As a narrative review, this study synthesizes diverse evidence but lacks the methodological rigor of a systematic review or meta-analysis. The conclusions are plausible but preliminary, given the absence of high-quality longitudinal or interventional data. The shift to dimensional frameworks is well-supported, but claims about the clinical utility of digital phenotyping and integrated interventions are based on emerging—not definitive—evidence. The review is useful for framing clinical questions but should not guide definitive practice changes.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Clinicians should consider the dimensional nature of PD-SUD comorbidity and adopt integrated, personality-informed approaches where feasible. However, treatment decisions should still rely on established guidelines until stronger evidence emerges. Watch for evolving tools like digital phenotyping, but their role in routine care remains unproven.

item.title: [10] Efficacy of stem cell-derived extracellular vesicles in animal models of autism spectrum disorder: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) lacks targeted therapies, and stem cell-derived extracellular vesicles (EVs) are being explored as a potential treatment in animal models. This systematic review and meta-analysis assessed the efficacy of EVs on autistic-like behaviors and inflammatory markers in ASD animal models.
FINDINGS: Five animal studies (total sample size not specified in abstract) were included. Pooled analyses showed EV treatment improved autistic-like behaviors in the self-grooming test (P < 0.05), three-chamber social interaction test (P < 0.05), and marble burying test (P < 0.05). EV treatment also decreased proinflammatory cytokines IL-6 and IL-1β (P < 0.05). No significant effects were observed for the open field test, Morris Water Maze, TNF-α, or IL-10 (P > 0.05).
INTERPRETATION: The evidence is very preliminary, based on a small number of heterogeneous animal studies with unclear sample sizes and potential biases (e.g., lack of blinding, randomization details not specified in abstract). While statistically significant effects were reported, the clinical relevance is uncertain due to the preclinical nature of the evidence and the absence of effect sizes or confidence intervals in the abstract. Mechanistic associations (e.g., reduced IL-6 and IL-1β) are suggestive but not definitive.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: This meta-analysis does not change clinical practice yet. Further high-quality preclinical studies and rigorous clinical trials are needed to confirm efficacy, safety, and mechanisms before considering EV therapy for ASD in humans.

item.title: [10] Antidepressant Discontinuation During Pregnancy and Risk of Mental Health-Related Emergencies.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This retrospective cohort study (2023–2024) examined whether discontinuing SSRIs/SNRIs during pregnancy increases mental health-related emergency department (ED) visits among 1,462 privately insured patients in Pennsylvania with pre-pregnancy depression/anxiety. The clinical question is whether antidepressant continuation vs discontinuation affects acute psychiatric crises during and after pregnancy.
FINDINGS: 17.8% had no fills during pregnancy and 64.6% had a >60-day gap; most discontinuations occurred in the first trimester (44.9%). Before pregnancy, ED visit rates were similar between groups. During pregnancy, discontinuation was linked to higher mental health-related ED visits in the second month (58 vs 37/1,000, P=.027) and ninth month (59 vs 29/1,000, P<.01). Postpartum, discontinuation was associated with higher ED visits within 8 months (32 vs 21/1,000, P=.02).
INTERPRETATION: The study suggests discontinuation increases acute psychiatric care needs, but limitations include retrospective design, reliance on claims data (no symptom severity, adherence verification, or confounding by indication), and lack of adjustment for key confounders (e.g., psychotherapy, social support). The absolute risk difference is modest (about 10–30 extra ED visits per 1,000), and findings may not generalize beyond privately insured U.S. populations. Causality cannot be inferred.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: These data support cautious continuation of antidepressants during pregnancy when clinically indicated, but do not mandate universal continuation. Shared decision-making should weigh risks of relapse against potential fetal exposure, with close monitoring for symptom exacerbation, especially in the first and third trimesters and early postpartum.

item.title: [9] Schema therapy for personality disorders.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This is a narrative review summarizing recent advances in schema therapy for personality disorders, focusing on theoretical developments, clinical effectiveness, mechanisms of change, and implementation. It synthesizes findings from recent trials and studies to assess the evidence base for schema therapy across different personality disorder subtypes.
FINDINGS: Recent trials continue to support schema therapy as an effective treatment for borderline personality disorder (BPD). Evidence is accumulating for its applicability to cluster C personality disorders and other personality disorder subtypes. Studies report clinically relevant changes in early maladaptive schemas and schema modes, particularly reductions in the Vulnerable Child mode and strengthening of the Healthy Adult mode. However, the causal role of these changes remains uncertain.
INTERPRETATION: The evidence base for schema therapy in personality disorders, particularly BPD, is growing and appears robust. The review highlights strengths in integrating developmental theory with experiential interventions, offering a distinctive therapeutic framework. However, as a narrative review, it lacks the rigor of a systematic review or meta-analysis, and the causal mechanisms of change remain unclear. The generalizability of findings, particularly across different cultural contexts, is also uncertain.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Schema therapy may be considered a viable treatment option for BPD and potentially other personality disorders, particularly cluster C. Clinicians should be aware that while symptom improvement and schema mode changes are reported, the mechanisms driving these changes are not fully understood. Further research is needed to clarify optimal delivery formats and cross-cultural applicability.

item.title: [7] Buccal and sublingual lyophilised naloxone for opioid overdose reversal: A Phase 1 open-label, random-sequence crossover pharmacokinetic study protocol in healthy volunteers (NalBuc).
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This Phase 1 open-label, randomized-sequence crossover pharmacokinetic (PK) study in 12–15 healthy UK adults will compare the absorption profile of a novel ultra-portable lyophilised naloxone wafer (2 mg and 4 mg buccal or sublingual) against intramuscular (0.4 mg) and intranasal (1.8 mg) comparators to assess whether mucosal delivery can achieve rapid systemic exposure.
FINDINGS: The primary endpoint is time to maximum plasma concentration (Tmax); secondary PK endpoints include Cmax, T50%, AUC0-15, and AUCinf. Safety and tolerability will also be monitored. No numerical results are reported in the abstract; the study is designed to characterise absorption and relative bioavailability rather than test pre-specified hypotheses.
INTERPRETATION: As a Phase 1 exploratory PK study without efficacy endpoints, internal validity hinges on robust crossover randomisation (≥36 h washout) and validated LC-MS/MS assays, but the open-label design and healthy-volunteer sample limit external validity to real-world overdose patients. The absence of clinical outcomes (e.g., reversal success) and small sample size preclude any inference about effectiveness or safety in overdose settings. Findings will guide, but not confirm, subsequent confirmatory trials.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: At present, this protocol offers no bedside-ready change; it merely signals a potential future delivery route for naloxone that warrants larger, blinded, patient-centred studies before any practice recommendation can be made.

item.title: [7] Adherence to the 24 h Movement Guidelines and Associated Factors Among First-Year University Students in Spain: UNILIFE-M Study at Universidad Loyola Andalucía.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: The study examined how many first-year university students in Spain met integrated 24-hour movement guidelines (physical activity, sedentary behaviour, sleep) and which factors were linked to adherence, using a cross-sectional design at a single university.
FINDINGS: Among 646 students, 21.2% met all three guidelines and 8.4% met none. Male sex was associated with higher odds of adherence (adjusted OR 1.65, 95% CI 1.10–2.47), while a lifetime mental health diagnosis was linked to lower odds (aOR 0.28, 95% CI 0.08–0.72). Age >18 years and non-health sciences enrolment showed borderline associations that were not robust in sensitivity analyses.
INTERPRETATION: The evidence is limited by its cross-sectional design, single-university setting, and self-reported behaviours, so causal inference is not possible. The associations are modest and may not reflect broader populations. The small effect sizes and borderline findings suggest limited clinical relevance at this stage.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Current findings do not justify practice changes but highlight a need for longitudinal research to clarify whether improving movement behaviours could benefit mental health in university students.

item.title: [7] A mixed methods study of perinatal depressive and anxiety symptom prevalence and the role of traditional healing alongside clinical care in Southern Malawi.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This convergent parallel mixed-methods study in Southern Malawi examined the prevalence of perinatal depressive and anxiety symptoms and the role of traditional healing alongside clinical care in a population where cultural beliefs strongly influence health-seeking behaviour.
FINDINGS: Among 330 perinatal mothers, 35% screened positive for moderate-to-severe depressive symptoms (PHQ-9 mean 10.5, SD 4.3) and 30% for moderate-to-severe anxiety (GAD-7 mean 9.2, SD 3.9). Sixty percent used traditional healing methods, while 40% reported barriers to clinical care such as stigma and limited awareness. Qualitative interviews with mothers, healthcare providers, and traditional healers highlighted complementary roles and system gaps.
INTERPRETATION: The study provides locally relevant prevalence estimates and highlights the coexistence of traditional and clinical care, but it relies on screening tools rather than clinical diagnoses and uses a non-probability sample. The qualitative component offers context but cannot establish causality or quantify effectiveness. Findings suggest potential for integrated care models, though evidence on safety, efficacy, and scalability remains limited.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Clinicians should be aware of high symptom prevalence and the prominent role of traditional healing in this setting. Integration efforts may improve access, but require careful evaluation to ensure evidence-based practice and avoid harm.

item.title: [7] Psychedelics and psychosis: A systematic review of recent-era studies (1984-2025).
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This systematic review (1984–2025) assessed whether classical psychedelics (LSD, psilocybin, DMT/ayahuasca, mescaline) precipitate psychotic symptoms, synthesizing 52 studies (one large cohort >100 000 participants and 34 case reports) to inform clinical risk assessment.
FINDINGS: Population-based data showed no consistent association between lifetime psychedelic use and psychosis. Across controlled clinical trials (n≈1000+ exposures), only one transient delusion was reported. Emergency/toxicology cohorts showed higher rates of psychotic symptoms, but these likely reflect selection of severe cases. In case reports (n=34), 58 % had prior psychiatric history; first-episode psychosis occurred rarely in otherwise healthy individuals.
INTERPRETATION: The evidence base is dominated by small, heterogeneous studies with high risk of confounding and publication bias. Large cohort data suggest no population-level increase in psychosis risk, while controlled trials under strict screening show minimal acute psychotic effects. Case reports highlight rare but real risks in vulnerable individuals or unsupervised settings. Causality cannot be established from observational data; selection bias inflates risk estimates in emergency samples. Overall certainty is low to moderate.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Current evidence does not support a general prohibition on psychedelic use in low-risk individuals, but it underscores the need for thorough psychiatric screening, structured settings, and post-session monitoring—especially for those with personal or family history of psychosis.

item.title: [6] Lower serum annexin A1 and neurogranin levels in chronic schizophrenia: a case-control study.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This single-centre case-control study examined whether serum levels of annexin A1 (ANXA1) and neurogranin (Ng) differ between 35 patients with chronic schizophrenia (DSM-5) and 35 healthy controls, motivated by hypotheses of synaptic dysfunction and immune dysregulation in schizophrenia.
FINDINGS: Median ANXA1 was 6.21 ng/mL (IQR 5.12–8.34) in patients vs. 13.06 ng/mL (8.82–23.66) in controls (U = 309, p = 3.6 × 10⁻⁴; rank-biserial r = −0.50). Median Ng was 174.2 pg/mL (149.1–281.0) vs. 380.0 pg/mL (237.1–547.1) (U = 302, p = 2.7 × 10⁻⁴; r = −0.51). Differences remained significant after Bonferroni/FDR correction and ANCOVA adjusting for age, sex and BMI (adjusted differences −6.71 ng/mL, p = 0.011; −182.3 pg/mL, p = 0.0008). Neither biomarker correlated with symptom severity (PANSS, CGI-S) or antipsychotic dose metrics.
INTERPRETATION: The study shows moderate-to-large effect-size reductions in both biomarkers in schizophrenia with robust statistical significance, but the cross-sectional design precludes causal inference. Key limitations include small sample, single-centre recruitment, lack of inflammatory or central measures, uniform antipsychotic exposure, and absence of longitudinal data. The strong inter-correlation of ANXA1 and Ng suggests shared peripheral pathways, yet their lack of association with clinical severity or treatment variables limits immediate clinical interpretability.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: These exploratory findings identify ANXA1 and Ng as candidate peripheral markers in chronic schizophrenia, but replication in larger, diverse cohorts with longitudinal follow-up and central/immune measures is required before any bedside application.

item.title: [6] Longitudinal Clinical and Functional Outcomes in Adult-Onset Delusional Disorder and Schizophrenia: A 10-Year Prospective Comparison Study.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This 10-year prospective cohort study compared diagnostic stability, clinical, functional, and cognitive outcomes between first-episode delusional disorder (DD) and schizophrenia (SZ) in an age-matched cohort (n=142), addressing a debated distinction in psychiatry with potential prognostic implications.
FINDINGS: Over 10 years, 41% (29/71) of DD cases transitioned to SZ, versus 3% (2/71) of SZ cases shifting diagnoses. Among those retaining original diagnoses (n=111), SZ showed more relapses (B=1.27, P=.012), hospitalizations (B=0.47, P=.050), hallucinations (B=3.35, P=.012), and perseverative errors (B=4.31, P=.040), while DD had poorer insight (B=-1.38, P=.002). Sensitivity analyses (complete cases n=82; deceased-excluded n=100) confirmed consistency.
INTERPRETATION: The study provides robust longitudinal evidence using multiple imputation and sensitivity analyses, suggesting high diagnostic instability in DD but comparable functional/cognitive outcomes between stable DD and SZ. Limitations include potential selection bias (exclusion of deceased/non-retained diagnoses) and unmeasured confounders (e.g., treatment adherence). The clinical differences (e.g., insight, hallucinations) are statistically significant but may not translate to major functional divergence.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Clinicians should anticipate diagnostic evolution in DD over a decade, particularly toward SZ, while stable DD and SZ may share similar long-term functional trajectories. Insight monitoring in DD and relapse prevention in SZ remain key targets.

item.title: [6] A multi-agent large language model framework for structured clinical interviewing and psychiatric screening: a proof-of-concept.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: Can a multi-agent large language model (LLM) framework reliably administer structured psychiatric interviews and produce screening decisions without human input? The study tests technical feasibility in a simulation-based evaluation across 15 neuropsychiatric modules and a red-flag classifier.
FINDINGS: In 1,350 simulated interviews, module-level decisions matched rule-based expected outcomes with 87.8 % concordance (95 % CI 85.9–89.6), sensitivity 88.9 % (95 % CI 86.5–91.2) and specificity 86.7 % (95 % CI 84.0–89.2). The multi-agent framework outperformed single-pass LLM (F2 88.5 % vs 49.5 %) and deterministic rule-based scoring (F2 61.9 %). A 2,000-sentence red-flag benchmark yielded 93.9 % accuracy, 94.2 % sensitivity and 93.6 % specificity. Clinician pilot feedback rated clarity, workflow fit and perceived safety positively.
INTERPRETATION: The evidence is preliminary (proof-of-concept simulation) with no real-world patient data or clinical outcomes. Internal validity is high for the technical task (predefined modules, rule-based comparators, clear metrics), but external validity is untested—no real patients, no diagnostic gold standard, and no clinical decision impact measured. Effect sizes are large for the benchmark tasks, yet clinical significance remains unknown until prospective studies in routine care demonstrate safety, equity and non-inferiority to human interviewers.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: This is a promising technical demonstration rather than a practice-changing study; clinicians should await real-world validation before considering any integration into screening workflows.

item.title: [29] Implementing Australia's psychotropic clinical practice guidelines in residential aged care: the EMBRACE helix counterbalanced randomised controlled trial comparing knowledge brokers with pharmacist education and passive distribution.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: The EMBRACE trial was a 12-month helix-counterbalanced RCT (Oct 2023–Sep 2024) in 19 Australian residential aged care facilities (RACFs) across four states. It tested three implementation strategies—passive guideline distribution (Level 1), pharmacist-led education (Level 2), and onsite knowledge broker pharmacist support (Level 3)—to reduce non-concordance with Australia’s psychotropic guidelines for residents with dementia.
FINDINGS: At the primary 6-month endpoint, there were no significant differences in overall guideline non-concordance between Level 3 vs Level 2 (difference −0.02, 95% CI −0.08 to 0.03, p=0.43) or Level 3 vs Level 1 (−0.03, 95% CI −0.08 to 0.03, p=0.34). No differences were seen at 3, 9, or 12 months or for specific recommendations. All three strategies showed a small but significant monthly reduction in non-concordance (Level 1: −0.004; Level 2: −0.006; Level 3: −0.006 per month). Costs per resident over 12 months were highest for Level 3 (AUD 207.53) and lowest for Level 1 (AUD 30.12).
INTERPRETATION: The trial provides moderate-quality evidence that none of the three implementation strategies outperformed the others in reducing guideline non-concordance. The observed time trend suggests secular improvement or Hawthorne effects rather than strategy-specific impact. Contamination between levels and the use of a composite outcome may have masked true differences. The cost differential favours simpler strategies, but the clinical benefit remains uncertain.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: For now, passive guideline dissemination appears sufficient to achieve modest reductions in inappropriate psychotropic use in RACFs, with no clear advantage to more resource-intensive approaches. Clinicians should continue to monitor prescribing patterns but need not prioritise knowledge broker interventions over simpler, lower-cost strategies.

item.title: [20] Real-world associations of antipsychotic use with clinical outcomes in schizophrenia: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This systematic review and meta-analysis examined observational studies on associations between antipsychotic use and clinical outcomes in individuals with schizophrenia, synthesizing evidence on mortality, somatic disorders, and other outcomes to inform treatment decisions.
FINDINGS: Sixty-eight observational studies (n=1,424,455) showed lower all-cause mortality (pooled HR 0.64, 95% CI 0.54–0.77) and relapse risk (HR 0.34, 95% CI 0.12–0.99) with antipsychotic use versus nonuse. However, antipsychotic use was linked to higher risks of cancer (HR 1.41, 95% CI 1.17–1.69), fractures (HR 1.35, 95% CI 1.17–1.56), and lung infections (HR 1.25, 95% CI 1.04–1.51). Many pooled estimates relied on few studies, and subgroup analyses suggested regional and design-related variability.
INTERPRETATION: The evidence is observational and prone to confounding and bias, limiting causal inference. While the direction of associations (benefits for mortality/relapse, harms for fractures/infections) is consistent, effect sizes may be over- or underestimated. The small number of studies for some outcomes and heterogeneity across subgroups further weaken certainty. Rigorous longitudinal or quasi-experimental designs are needed to clarify causality and quantify absolute risks.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Current findings support antipsychotics’ role in reducing mortality and relapse but warrant vigilance for adverse outcomes like fractures and infections. Clinicians should balance benefits against risks, monitor high-risk patients, and avoid overgeneralizing from pooled estimates with limited data.

item.title: [20] Music-based interventions for people with kidney failure undergoing haemodialysis.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: A Cochrane systematic review assessed whether music-based interventions reduce fatigue, blood pressure, depression, pain, anxiety, stress, quality of life, and sleep quality in adults receiving haemodialysis for kidney failure, synthesising 27 RCTs (n=1584) with outcomes stratified by short- (<4 weeks), medium- (4 weeks–6 months), and long-term (>6 months).
FINDINGS: Low-certainty evidence suggests music-based interventions may reduce short-term fatigue (MD −3.14 on 10-point scale, 95% CI −3.83 to −2.45; 1 study, 62 participants) and short-term pain (SMD −0.89, 95% CI −1.63 to −0.15; 8 studies, 675 participants). Low-certainty evidence also indicates possible short- and medium-term reductions in depressive symptoms (short-term SMD −0.88, 95% CI −1.51 to −0.25; 6 studies, 489 participants; medium-term SMD −0.81, 95% CI −1.42 to −0.19; 5 studies, 203 participants). Effects on blood pressure were very uncertain (short-term MD −5.95 mmHg, 95% CI −10.56 to −1.34; 8 studies, 674 participants; very low certainty). No long-term data were available for any critical outcome.
INTERPRETATION: The evidence base is limited by small sample sizes, heterogeneity (I² up to 92%), and predominantly low to very low GRADE certainty, especially for medium-term outcomes. While point estimates suggest potential benefits for fatigue, pain, and depression, the clinical significance of these effects is uncertain given wide confidence intervals and risk of bias. The absence of long-term data precludes conclusions about durability. Funding sources were academic and unlikely to bias results, but the review highlights a clear need for larger, rigorously designed RCTs with longer follow-up.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Current evidence does not justify routine implementation of music-based interventions for symptom control in haemodialysis patients; any adoption should be cautious, monitored for patient-centred outcomes, and considered within shared decision-making pending higher-quality trials.

item.title: [12] [Advances in the efficacy of digital psychological therapies for depressive disorders].
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This narrative review synthesizes evidence on the efficacy of digital psychological therapies (e.g., internet-based CBT) for depressive disorders, highlighting variability in effect sizes and the gap between efficacy and real-world effectiveness. It examines intervention characteristics, participant populations, and control conditions as sources of heterogeneity.
FINDINGS: Reported effect sizes (Hedges' g) range from 0.22 to 1.01 in efficacy studies, with a pooled estimate of g=0.59, but drop to g=0.30 in real-world effectiveness studies. Human guidance improves outcomes, but optimal guidance format (on-demand, scheduled, intensive) and provider qualifications remain unclear. Evidence is limited for older adults, severe depression, and comorbid populations. Wait-list controls may inflate effect estimates compared to treatment-as-usual or psychological placebos.
INTERPRETATION: The review underscores substantial heterogeneity and potential overestimation of effects in controlled trials. Strengths include a broad synthesis of sources of variability, but limitations include lack of quantitative pooling and reliance on narrative methods. The clinical significance of guidance format and provider qualifications is uncertain due to insufficient comparative data. The drop from efficacy to effectiveness suggests real-world barriers (e.g., adherence, comorbidity) are critical but understudied.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Digital therapies show promise, especially with human support, but effect sizes in practice may be modest. Clinicians should prioritize guided programs and monitor adherence, particularly in older or severely ill patients, while recognizing evidence gaps for these groups. Standardized reporting and long-term follow-up are needed before firm recommendations can be made.

item.title: [9] Electroacupuncture Combined with Cognitive Behavioral Therapy for Insomnia Alleviates Insomnia-Anxiety Comorbidity in Gynecological Cancer Patients Undergoing Chemotherapy: A Randomized Controlled Trial.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This randomized controlled trial (RCT) tested whether adding electroacupuncture (EA) to cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia (CBT-I) improves sleep and anxiety in gynecological cancer patients undergoing chemotherapy, a population with limited non-pharmacological options.
FINDINGS: In 76 patients, after 4 weeks, the EA + CBT-I group showed a greater reduction in PSQI global score (mean difference in change: -3.11, 95% CI: -4.11 to -2.11, p < 0.001). More patients achieved insomnia remission (AIS ≤ 6: 71.1% vs. 42.1%, p = 0.010) and anxiety remission (HAMA ≤ 14: 92.1% vs. 65.8%, p = 0.005). Objective sleep parameters (deep sleep, REM sleep, sleep score) also improved more with EA. The overall response rate was higher in the EA group (92.1% vs. 71.1%, p = 0.016). No serious adverse events were reported.
INTERPRETATION: The study provides moderate-quality evidence that adding EA to CBT-I improves sleep and anxiety outcomes in this specific population. Strengths include the RCT design, objective sleep measures, and clear statistical significance. However, the sample size is modest, follow-up is short (4 weeks), and blinding integrity may be compromised (sham EA as control). The clinical significance of a PSQI reduction of ~3 points is uncertain without patient-centered anchors. Longer-term follow-up and replication in broader settings are needed.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: EA may be a useful adjunct to CBT-I for insomnia and anxiety in gynecological cancer patients on chemotherapy, but evidence is preliminary. Clinicians should weigh benefits against feasibility and patient preferences, pending larger, longer-term trials.

item.title: [7] Uptake of Annual Health Checks in Primary Care for People with Severe Mental Illness: A Systematic Review and Qualitative Synthesis.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: People with severe mental illness (SMI) face higher risks of poor physical health and premature death. While annual physical health checks in primary care are recommended, uptake is low and reasons for this are unclear. This systematic review and qualitative synthesis explored experiences of annual health checks among people with SMI, carers, and primary care providers.
FINDINGS: Eight qualitative studies from five countries (N=375 participants) identified five key themes: understanding of the purpose of health checks; individual, relational, and service-level barriers to uptake; quality of clinical interactions; constraints on behaviour change; and service-level enablers. Barriers included lack of awareness, stigma, fragmented care, and limited continuity with providers. Enablers included trusting relationships, flexible scheduling, and proactive outreach.
INTERPRETATION: The evidence base is small (8 studies, 375 participants) and heterogeneous in setting, limiting generalisability. Thematic synthesis provides insight into multilevel barriers and facilitators but cannot quantify uptake or effectiveness. The findings are plausible and clinically relevant but preliminary; stronger evidence (e.g., mixed-methods or implementation studies) is needed to guide policy and practice.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Current findings suggest that improving uptake requires addressing stigma, enhancing continuity of care, and tailoring services to patient needs. Clinicians should focus on building trust and offering flexible, proactive health checks, but should await further evidence before expecting major system-wide changes.

item.title: [25] Educational Interventions for Perinatal Depression Management Among Non-Specialist Providers in Resource-Constrained Settings: A Descriptive Systematic Review of Limited Evidence.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: A descriptive systematic review examined educational interventions for non-specialist providers managing perinatal depression (PND) in resource-constrained settings, synthesizing quasi-experimental studies published between 2019–2025 across Nigeria, Saudi Arabia, and Thailand.
FINDINGS: Three non-randomized studies (n=351) were included, all judged to be at critical risk of bias using ROBINS-I V2. Educational models commonly used WHO mhGAP frameworks and multi-session, cascade training with mobile supervision, showing improvements in provider-level metrics. No studies assessed patient outcomes, and high attrition and lack of control groups precluded causal inference.
INTERPRETATION: The evidence base is extremely limited, methodologically weak, and insufficient to determine whether educational interventions improve PND care or outcomes. The narrative synthesis highlights feasibility and training structure but cannot support clinical recommendations due to critical risk of bias and absence of patient-centered data.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Current findings are hypothesis-generating only; routine adoption of these educational models in perinatal depression care is not supported by evidence. High-quality randomized or quasi-experimental trials with patient outcomes are urgently needed before implementation.

item.title: [15] Combining Cognitive Training and Brain Stimulation: A Novel Approach to Address Disordered Eating and Antipsychotic-Induced Weight Gain in People With Severe Mental Illness.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This double-blind, sham-controlled RCT tested whether five sessions of Approach Bias Modification Training (ABMT) combined with real or sham transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS) over 3 weeks could reduce food craving and binge eating in adults with schizophrenia/schizoaffective disorder on stable antipsychotics.
FINDINGS: Twenty-eight participants were randomised (93 % of target). Retention was 85.7 % at post-treatment and 78.6 % at 2-week follow-up; blinding accuracy was 46.4 %. Medium effect sizes favoured ABMT + real tDCS for binge eating (d = –0.6, 95 % CI –1.5 to 0.3) and ABMT + sham tDCS for food cravings (d = 0.5, 95 % CI –0.4 to 1.4). Within-group analyses showed reduced approach bias to food and increased avoidance bias only in the real-tDCS arm (all p < 0.05), followed by fewer binge-eating episodes (p < 0.05).
INTERPRETATION: The study demonstrates feasibility and acceptability, with high recruitment and retention, but the small sample and wide confidence intervals mean the apparent medium effects are highly uncertain. The within-group changes suggest a possible synergistic effect of ABMT + real tDCS on approach-avoidance bias, but the absence of a between-group statistical difference precludes firm conclusions. A larger, adequately powered confirmatory trial with stratification by binge-eating disorder diagnosis is needed.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Current evidence is insufficient to change practice; the combination may be worth exploring in selected patients, but clinicians should await robust efficacy data before adopting ABMT + tDCS for antipsychotic-induced weight gain.

item.title: [15] Effect of Probiotics on GI Symptom Management in Autism Spectrum Disorder: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Clinical Trials.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This systematic review and meta-analysis examined whether probiotics reduce gastrointestinal (GI) symptoms in individuals with autism spectrum disorder (ASD), a population with high rates of GI comorbidity and proposed gut-brain axis dysfunction. Six clinical trials comparing probiotics (single or multiple strains) to placebo were pooled.
FINDINGS: The overall pooled effect showed a small, non-significant reduction in GI symptoms with probiotics (SMD = −0.189; 95% CI −0.398 to 0.020; p = 0.07; I² = 39.4%). Subgroup analysis suggested single-strain probiotics may modestly improve GI symptoms versus placebo, while multiple-strain formulations did not differ significantly from placebo.
INTERPRETATION: The evidence is preliminary and limited by moderate heterogeneity and a small total sample size. The borderline p-value and small effect size suggest any benefit is likely modest at best. Risk of bias and variability in strains/doses across trials further weaken conclusions. Larger, rigorously designed RCTs with standardized probiotic formulations are needed before clinical recommendations can be made.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Current evidence does not support routine use of probiotics for GI symptoms in ASD. Clinicians should remain cautious about recommending probiotics until higher-quality trials confirm efficacy and define optimal strains/doses.

item.title: [15] Clinical practice guidelines for managing psychosocial difficulties in adults with moderate-to-severe traumatic brain injury: considerations for people from culturally and linguistically diverse backgrounds.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This clinical practice guideline addresses how to manage psychosocial difficulties in adults with moderate-to-severe traumatic brain injury (TBI) from culturally and linguistically diverse (CALD) backgrounds, a group reported to have poorer functional and mental health outcomes. The recommendations were developed using qualitative interviews with CALD individuals with TBI, additional consultations, and integration of existing cultural guidelines in mental health.
FINDINGS: The guideline emphasizes cultural competency training for clinicians, consideration of acculturation levels and migration impacts, culturally sensitive communication (including interpreter use), and understanding psychosocial challenges through a cultural lens. Recommendations are based on qualitative data and expert consultation rather than quantitative outcomes.
INTERPRETATION: The strength of this guideline lies in its grounding in qualitative evidence from the target population, highlighting barriers such as stigma, isolation, and communication challenges. However, the lack of quantitative data (e.g., effect sizes, confidence intervals) limits the ability to assess the impact of these recommendations on clinical outcomes. The process involved only a small number of participants and relied heavily on expert consultation, which may introduce bias. External validity is uncertain due to the specific context of CALD individuals with TBI in Australia.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Clinicians should consider integrating culturally sensitive practices into care plans for CALD patients with TBI, such as using interpreters and assessing acculturation levels. However, the recommendations are based on qualitative insights rather than robust evidence, so their implementation should be monitored for effectiveness in routine care.

item.title: [12] Moving towards evidence-based screening and investigations in first episode psychosis: A commentary on the ANZJP GRADE Schizophrenia Guidelines.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: The commentary critiques the ANZJP GRADE Schizophrenia Guidelines, which provide evidence-based recommendations for routine physical health investigations in first episode psychosis (FEP). It highlights gaps in addressing affective psychosis and sexual health screening, emphasizing the need for comprehensive physical health assessment in this population.
FINDINGS: The guidelines prioritize diagnostic clarification and monitoring for iatrogenic harms but may underemphasize sexual health and affective psychosis. The commentary argues that people with FEP represent a high-risk group for sexually transmitted infections (STIs), warranting broader screening than currently recommended.
INTERPRETATION: This is a commentary (not primary research), so it synthesizes existing guidelines rather than presenting new data. Strengths include addressing a critical gap in FEP care, but limitations include lack of quantitative evidence and reliance on expert opinion. The clinical implications depend on whether affective psychosis and STIs are clinically significant in FEP—further research is needed to quantify risks and refine recommendations.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Clinicians should remain vigilant for sexual health issues and affective psychosis in FEP, even if current guidelines do not mandate routine screening. Further evidence may justify broader investigations in these subgroups.

item.title: [7] Expert guidance to inform coordinated suicide postvention responses: A Delphi study.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: The study aimed to establish expert consensus on best practices for implementing Postvention Protocol Response Groups (PPRGs)—coordinated local services supporting communities after a suicide—using a Delphi method with 30 Australian experts (PPRG members, postvention specialists, and bereaved individuals). The clinical question was how to optimally structure PPRGs to enhance their effectiveness and sustainability.
FINDINGS: The Delphi panel endorsed 126 statements (rated ≥80% as "essential" or "important") covering stakeholder engagement, governance, operational practices, data surveillance, and rural-specific considerations. No quantitative effect sizes or statistical tests were reported; the results reflect consensus-based recommendations rather than empirical outcomes.
INTERPRETATION: The study’s strength lies in its structured consensus-building among diverse experts, offering practical guidance for PPRG implementation. However, as a Delphi study, it lacks external validation or measurable outcomes, relying solely on expert opinion. The recommendations are preliminary and may not generalize beyond the Australian context or to non-specialist settings. No clinical significance can be inferred without follow-up studies assessing real-world impact.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: This guidance may inform the development of PPRGs in new regions or improve existing programs, but clinicians should await empirical evidence before assuming these practices will improve postvention outcomes. Implementation should be piloted with careful monitoring of feasibility and impact.

item.title: [6] Genome-wide analysis identifies pleiotropic genes shared between severe mental disorders and biomarkers of cellular aging.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This genome-wide association study (GWAS) examined genetic overlap between severe mental disorders (bipolar disorder, major depressive disorder, schizophrenia) and biomarkers of cellular aging (e.g., telomere length, epigenetic age acceleration) to explore whether shared heritability contributes to reduced longevity in these conditions.
FINDINGS: All three disorders showed negative genetic correlation with multivariate longevity/healthy aging (mvAge). Major depressive disorder (MDD) additionally showed negative correlation with leukocyte telomere length (gLTL) and positive correlation with epigenetic age acceleration (gEAA). Nine pleiotropic genes were identified across all disorders and aging biomarkers. Functional analyses implicated increased CRHR1 expression in the prefrontal cortex as potentially increasing risk for MDD and brain age gap (BAG).
INTERPRETATION: This study provides preliminary genetic evidence linking severe mental disorders with cellular aging processes, suggesting shared biological pathways. However, as a GWAS relying on summary-level data, causal inference is limited and effect sizes are not quantified. The findings are hypothesis-generating and require experimental validation. The clinical relevance of identified genes remains uncertain.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: No immediate change in practice is warranted. These findings may guide future research into mechanisms of accelerated aging in psychiatric disorders and potential therapeutic targets, but translation to patient care is not yet possible.

item.title: [6] HINT1 in ventral hippocampal GABAergic neurons mediates depressive-like behaviors.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This preclinical mouse study examined whether histidine trimeric nucleotide-binding protein 1 (HINT1) in ventral hippocampal GABAergic neurons contributes to depressive-like behaviors after chronic social defeat stress (CSDS), a model of depression-like states in animals.
FINDINGS: Susceptible mice showed ~1.5–2-fold upregulation of HINT1 in hippocampus and mPFC. Targeted vHip HINT1 overexpression increased depressive-like behaviors (e.g., social avoidance p < 0.01, sucrose preference decrease p < 0.05), whereas vHip HINT1 knockdown reversed deficits (effect sizes not reported). The selective HINT1 inhibitor TpGc infused into vHip normalized behavior and neuronal firing. Cell-type work implicated SST+ and PV+ GABAergic neurons; HINT1 overexpression in these subtypes worsened phenotypes. Proteomics linked HINT1 to upregulation of the SUMO E3 ligase CBX4 (~1.8-fold), and CBX4 overexpression in GABAergic vHip neurons induced depressive-like behavior. Mechanistically, HINT1 inhibited PKCβ1 phosphorylation, dampening MEK1/2-ERK1/2 signaling, increasing CBX4, and altering GluN2A SUMOylation and trafficking.
INTERPRETATION: The study uses a robust CSDS paradigm with targeted viral manipulations and pharmacological inhibition, supporting a causal role for HINT1 in vHip GABAergic neurons in depressive-like behaviors. Limitations include lack of effect-size estimates, absence of human data, and reliance on a single stress model in mice. The mechanistic cascade (HINT1→PKCβ1→ERK→CBX4→GluN2A SUMOylation) is plausible but needs replication and translational validation. Overall, the evidence is preliminary but points to HINT1 as a potential upstream regulator warranting further study.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: These findings do not yet change practice; they suggest HINT1 and downstream SUMO pathways as future drug targets. Clinicians should watch for emerging translational studies linking HINT1 biology to human depression before considering any therapeutic implications.

item.title: [6] Substance use disorder, psychiatric illness, and suicide risk among hospitalized incarcerated adults: A retrospective study using National Inpatient Sample (NIS) database.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: The study used a large U.S. claims database (NIS 2016-2021) to examine how substance use disorder (SUD) in hospitalized incarcerated adults is linked to psychiatric comorbidity, suicidality, and hospital outcomes in a retrospective cohort.
FINDINGS: Among 92,715 hospitalized incarcerated adults, 40.4 % had SUD. Suicidal ideation was present in 75.4 % of those with SUD versus 38.6 % without (aOR 3.73, p < .001). SUD was also associated with higher odds of major depressive disorder (aOR 1.43), schizophrenia-spectrum (aOR 1.61), bipolar (aOR 1.66), anxiety (aOR 2.07), trauma-related (aOR 1.90), and personality disorders (aOR 1.63; all p < .001). SUD was linked to lower in-hospital mortality and lower total charges, with no difference in length of stay.
INTERPRETATION: The large sample and clear associations strengthen confidence that SUD co-occurs with severe psychiatric morbidity and suicidality in this population. However, the retrospective design, reliance on ICD-10 codes, and lack of adjustment for unmeasured confounders (e.g., severity of incarceration, prior treatment) limit causal inference. The lower charges and mortality may reflect selection or coding artifacts rather than true clinical benefit. Effect sizes for psychiatric diagnoses are modest despite statistical significance.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Incarcerated inpatients with SUD merit routine, integrated psychiatric screening and suicide risk assessment during hospitalization; current findings do not yet justify specific treatment changes beyond standard dual-diagnosis care.

item.title: [22] Management of shift work disorder: an American Academy of Sleep Medicine clinical practice guideline.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This American Academy of Sleep Medicine (AASM) clinical practice guideline uses a systematic review and GRADE methodology to evaluate treatments for shift work disorder (SWD) in adults, focusing on excessive sleepiness and/or insomnia symptoms. It provides conditional recommendations based on very low to moderate certainty evidence.
FINDINGS: The guideline conditionally recommends modafinil/armodafinil for excessive sleepiness (moderate certainty), bright light therapy (very low certainty), caffeine (very low certainty), clockwise rotating shifts (very low certainty), and pre-shift naps (very low certainty). For insomnia, it conditionally recommends CBT-I (very low certainty), melatonin (very low to low certainty), ramelteon/suvorexant (low certainty), and advises against benzodiazepines (very low certainty). For circadian adaptation, bright light with fixed sleep timing and morning light-blocking glasses are suggested (very low certainty). No preference is given for 8-hour vs. 12-hour night shifts (very low certainty).
INTERPRETATION: The evidence base is weak (mostly very low certainty), with only modafinil/armodafinil backed by moderate certainty. Recommendations are conditional, emphasizing shared decision-making due to limited high-quality trials. Harms (e.g., sleep inertia with naps/melatonin) and impracticality for rotating shifts are noted. External validity is limited by study populations (often healthy shift workers) and short follow-ups.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Modafinil/armodafinil may modestly help excessive sleepiness in SWD, but other interventions (bright light, caffeine, CBT-I) have uncertain benefits. Clinicians should prioritize sleep hygiene, nap safety, and avoid benzodiazepines for insomnia. Rotating-shift workers may not benefit from circadian adaptation strategies.

item.title: [21] Efficacy and safety of GLP-1 receptor agonists in patients with schizophrenia spectrum disorders treated with antipsychotics: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This systematic review and meta-analysis of seven RCTs (n=481) assessed the efficacy and safety of GLP-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1 RAs) versus placebo in patients with schizophrenia spectrum disorders (SSD) treated with antipsychotics, focusing on weight, metabolic, and psychiatric outcomes.
FINDINGS: GLP-1 RAs significantly reduced body weight (MD -6.98 kg; 95% CI -10.53 to -3.43), BMI (MD -2.51 kg/m²; 95% CI -3.51 to -1.51), waist circumference (MD -5.05 cm; 95% CI -6.66 to -3.44), HbA1c (MD -0.32 percentage points; 95% CI -0.38 to -0.26), and fasting glucose (MD -0.54 mmol/L; 95% CI -0.83 to -0.25). Psychiatric symptoms did not differ between groups (SMD -0.05; 95% CI -0.36 to 0.25). Gastrointestinal adverse events were more frequent with GLP-1 RAs, but overall dropout rates were similar. Heterogeneity was substantial for weight-related outcomes (I² up to 93%).
INTERPRETATION: The evidence suggests GLP-1 RAs improve short-term metabolic parameters in SSD patients, but the high heterogeneity, small sample size, and lack of long-term data limit confidence. The absence of psychiatric symptom improvement suggests the benefits are primarily metabolic. Further large-scale, longer-duration RCTs are needed to confirm efficacy, safety, and generalisability.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: GLP-1 RAs may be considered for managing antipsychotic-induced weight gain/metabolic dysfunction in SSD, but clinicians should monitor for gastrointestinal side effects and await more robust evidence before widespread adoption.

item.title: [20] Adjunctive Atypical Antipsychotics in Major Depressive Disorder: A Network Meta-Analysis Perspective and Consensus Panel Discussion.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This expert consensus panel synthesised comparative evidence from two recent network meta-analyses (NMAs) on FDA-approved atypical antipsychotics as adjuncts for adults with major depressive disorder (MDD) and inadequate antidepressant response, aiming to guide clinical decision-making.
FINDINGS: The panel discussed two NMAs that evaluated efficacy, acceptability, and safety of adjunctive atypical antipsychotics in MDD. While the NMAs used different inclusion criteria, treatment-node definitions, and analytical approaches, their comparative findings were broadly concordant. The panel highlighted the need to integrate efficacy with tolerability, patient preferences, and practical considerations when selecting treatments, and recommended earlier consideration of effective adjunctive options when appropriate.
INTERPRETATION: The strength of this consensus lies in the expert synthesis of comparative NMA data, providing a broad overview of relative efficacy and safety. However, the evidence base is indirect (network meta-analytic), and the panel’s conclusions are based on limited methodological detail provided in the abstract. Important limitations include heterogeneity in NMA approaches, lack of head-to-head trials, and limited long-term or phenotype-specific data. The clinical applicability depends heavily on individual patient profiles and local formulary availability.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: This consensus supports considering FDA-approved atypical antipsychotics as adjunctive therapy in MDD when antidepressants are insufficient, but does not endorse any specific agent. Clinicians should weigh efficacy against side-effect profiles and patient preferences, and remain cautious due to the lack of direct comparative evidence and long-term safety data.

item.title: [20] Efficacy of Non-Invasive Brain Stimulation on the Treatment of Late Life Depression: A Systematic Review and Network Meta-Analysis.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This systematic review and network meta-analysis (NMA) evaluated the comparative efficacy of non-invasive brain stimulation (NIBS) interventions for late-life depression (LLD) in adults aged ≥60 years, addressing a gap in evidence for this population through randomized controlled trials (RCTs).
FINDINGS: Twenty-five RCTs (n=1344) comparing 15 NIBS modalities were included. Bilateral electroconvulsive therapy (BL-ECT; SMD=1.13, 95% CI 0.37–1.90) and high-frequency rTMS over the left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (rTMS-10Hz-F3; SMD=0.42, 95% CI 0.02–0.81) showed statistically significant superiority over sham for depressive symptom reduction. Both interventions retained moderate-certainty evidence despite detected inconsistency in the symptom severity network.
INTERPRETATION: The evidence base is moderate in certainty and derived from RCTs, but the network meta-analytic approach introduces assumptions about indirect comparisons and loop consistency. BL-ECT shows a large effect size but is invasive and typically reserved for severe/refractory cases; rTMS-10Hz-F3 shows a smaller but clinically plausible effect. Other modalities ranked highly lacked robust data, limiting firm conclusions. The detected inconsistency warrants cautious interpretation of comparative rankings.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: BL-ECT and high-frequency left-dorsolateral prefrontal rTMS remain the most evidence-supported NIBS options for LLD, though BL-ECT is generally reserved for severe or treatment-resistant depression. Clinicians should prioritize these modalities in appropriate candidates, while recognizing that evidence for other NIBS techniques remains preliminary.

item.title: [15] Psychoeducation for posttraumatic stress disorder in adults: a systematic review of formats and delivery approaches.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This systematic review examined randomized controlled trials (RCTs) assessing the efficacy of psychoeducation—delivered alone or as a primary component—for adults with posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD), aiming to identify effective formats and delivery approaches.
FINDINGS: Twenty-six RCTs (n=3,304) were included. Nine trials reported significant reductions in PTSD symptoms attributable to psychoeducation, with all positive trials using digital delivery and most including some form of human guidance. Effects were inconsistent across studies, and several positive trials showed concerns or high risk of bias. Additional benefits were seen in perceived stress, anxiety, stigma, and help-seeking intentions.
INTERPRETATION: The evidence base is limited by heterogeneity in interventions, inconsistent outcomes, and risk of bias in several trials. While digital psychoeducation with human support shows promise, the overall effect on core PTSD symptoms is modest and inconsistent. The methodological quality and external validity are constrained by unregistered review processes and variable comparator groups.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Psychoeducation should not be used as a stand-alone treatment for PTSD but may serve as a useful first step in stepped-care models to improve engagement and reduce stigma. Clinicians should prioritize evidence-based trauma-focused therapies while considering psychoeducation as an adjunct, especially in digital formats with guided support.

item.title: [14] Treatment interventions for co-occurring opioid use disorder, and sleep disturbances: a scoping review.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This scoping review addresses the understudied intersection of opioid use disorder (OUD), sleep disturbances, and co-occurring psychiatric symptoms (depression, anxiety, PTSD) using PRISMA-ScR guidelines. It synthesizes pharmacological and non-pharmacological interventions targeting sleep in adults with OUD or opioid dependence, aiming to clarify treatment gaps and clinical relevance.
FINDINGS: Fifteen studies (n=1,167) were included, primarily adjunctive to opioid substitution or antagonist therapies. Naltrexone-induced insomnia was common but did not significantly worsen mood; lorazepam mitigated insomnia. Non-opioid pharmacotherapies showed mixed results: guanfacine increased insomnia risk but reduced stress/craving; amitriptyline, prazepam, dronabinol, and neurotransmitter-precursor supplements showed potential for sleep/withdrawal improvement.
INTERPRETATION: The evidence base is limited (heterogeneous studies, small samples, no RCTs), precluding firm conclusions. Methodological weaknesses (lack of blinding, high dropout, varied comparators) and unclear funding sources reduce internal validity. External validity is constrained by diverse interventions and populations. The clinical significance of observed effects remains uncertain due to inconsistent outcomes and absence of standardized sleep metrics.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Current findings suggest sleep disturbances in OUD warrant attention, but no definitive treatment recommendations can be made. Clinicians should monitor sleep as part of OUD care while awaiting higher-quality evidence. Integrated, patient-centered approaches are justified but require further research to optimize interventions.

item.title: [10] From Hospital to Outpatient Care After Long-Acting Injectable Antipsychotic Initiation in Bipolar Disorder: Nationwide Evidence From Taiwan.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: The study examined whether initiating second-generation long-acting injectable antipsychotics (SGA-LAIs) in patients with bipolar disorder (BD) in Taiwan shifts healthcare utilization from acute to outpatient settings, using nationwide retrospective data. The mirror-image design compared the 12 months before and after SGA-LAI initiation.
FINDINGS: Among 17,513 SGA-LAI initiators, 2,937 had BD, and 500 stable users were analyzed. After initiation, both stable and nonstable users showed increased psychiatric outpatient visits (e.g., +X% in stable users) and expenditures, alongside reduced emergency department (ED) visits (e.g., -Y%) and inpatient admissions (e.g., -Z%). The shift toward ambulatory care was more pronounced in stable users.
INTERPRETATION: The study’s mirror-image design and large nationwide sample strengthen internal validity, but the lack of randomization and reliance on administrative data introduce confounding (e.g., unmeasured clinical severity). The focus on healthcare utilization—not relapse or symptom outcomes—limits conclusions about clinical efficacy. The "stable use" subgroup analysis reflects implementation fidelity rather than drug efficacy. Confidence in the findings is moderate due to potential residual confounding and generalizability limited to Taiwan’s single-payer system.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: SGA-LAI initiation in BD may reduce acute-care reliance and increase outpatient engagement, particularly with sustained use. However, this does not confirm superior efficacy over oral antipsychotics; rather, it suggests better continuity of care with LAIs in this setting. Clinicians should weigh these utilization shifts against costs, patient preferences, and alternatives.

item.title: [10] An Individual Meta-Analysis of Psychological Treatments for Mood and Personality Disorders Using the Severity Diagnostic System of ICD-11.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: The study used an individual patient meta-analysis of four RCTs (n=1,384) to test whether ICD-11 personality-disorder severity levels (none → personality difficulty → moderate → severe) differentially predict short-term (12–24 m) outcomes after psychological treatments (mostly CBT) versus control conditions for mood/anxiety symptoms and social function.
FINDINGS: Higher ICD-11 severity was linearly associated with worse baseline mood/anxiety symptoms; moderate and severe PD groups showed significantly less improvement in anxiety than the no-PD group (effect sizes not reported). Depressive-symptom change was inconsistent across trials. Social function improved in all groups. Treatment effects were small and did not differ by PD severity.
INTERPRETATION: The evidence is moderate in quality (pooled individual-level data from four RCTs, but proxy PD severity measures and no formal severity-by-treatment interaction test). The consistent baseline gradient supports the dimensional ICD-11 PD severity model, but the lack of differential treatment response limits clinical utility. Small effect sizes and heterogeneity in depressive outcomes suggest results are preliminary rather than definitive.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Current evidence does not justify tailoring psychological treatment intensity by ICD-11 PD severity; standard CBT remains appropriate while further trials with validated PD severity measures are awaited.

item.title: [9] Metabolic biomarker levels before and after initiation of GLP-1 receptor agonist treatment among individuals with schizophrenia: interrupted time-series analysis.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: Observational register-based study examining whether initiating GLP-1 receptor agonist (GLP-1RA) treatment in real-world patients with schizophrenia leads to reductions in HbA1c, LDL and triglycerides, addressing the gap between RCT efficacy and routine care effectiveness.
FINDINGS: Among 3042 individuals with schizophrenia initiating GLP-1RA, HbA1c fell by 11.4% (diabetes indication) and 3.4% (overweight indication), LDL by 6.2% and 4.9%, and triglycerides by 14.8% and 12.7%, respectively; all changes were statistically significant (p < 0.001).
INTERPRETATION: Strengths include large nationwide sample and real-world design; however, lack of a comparator group, potential confounding by indication, and absence of data on medication adherence or lifestyle changes limit causal inference. The magnitude of change is modest and may not translate into clinically meaningful cardiovascular risk reduction for all patients.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Findings support considering GLP-1RA for metabolic risk in schizophrenia, but decisions should be individualised and balanced against side-effects and cost; ongoing monitoring of metabolic parameters remains essential.

item.title: [8] Assessing Suicide Risk Reduction in the Interval Before Death by Suicide Using Natural Language Processing.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This exploratory cohort study used natural language processing (NLP) to compare care patterns in the 6 months before suicide among U.S. Veterans Affairs (VA) patients whose high suicide-risk status was removed shortly before death (Reduced Clinical Risk Classification, RCRC, n=89) versus those whose high-risk status persisted (Sustained Clinical Risk Classification, SCRC, n=89).
FINDINGS: RCRC patients were younger and had fewer psychiatric diagnoses. Topic modeling identified psychotherapy-related terms (“Psychotherapy,” “Follow-up”) in RCRC records and medically structured terms (“Medication,” “Outpatient,” “Suicide-Assessment”) in SCRC records. After risk declassification, RCRC patients showed sharp declines across all topics, whereas SCRC patients maintained or increased engagement.
INTERPRETATION: The study is small, retrospective, and VA-specific, limiting generalisability to other settings. NLP-derived lexical patterns suggest contrasting care trajectories, but causality cannot be inferred. The observed dichotomy may reflect perceived improvement leading to reduced surveillance rather than true risk reduction. Larger, prospective studies with clinician-rated outcomes are needed to validate these findings and assess clinical significance.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Current evidence does not justify changing practice; clinicians should remain vigilant for subtle risk changes even when structured risk assessments suggest improvement.

item.title: [7] Polygenicity shapes distinct brain patterns and clinical profiles of bipolar disorder.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This multi-cohort, multi-ancestry genetic-neuroimaging study asks whether polygenic risk for bipolar disorder (BD) in East Asian populations maps onto specific brain imaging-derived phenotypes (IDPs) and whether these genetic-brain links carry clinical meaning. It integrates individual-level and summary-level data from >10 000 participants to perform cross-trait meta-analysis, fine-mapping, Mendelian randomisation and phenome-wide analyses.
FINDINGS: Eleven pleiotropic SNVs were identified across BD-IDP pairs, enriched for lipid metabolism and neurotransmitter pathways. An East-Asian-specific signal (rs7941324 near RPS27P20) showed high posterior inclusion probability only in EAS. Bidirectional Mendelian randomisation implicated 27 IDP→BD and 35 BD→IDP causal relationships; parietal/temporal gyri changes appeared pre-onset while right precuneus change tracked disease state. Polygenic risk scores combining BD-IDP signals correlated with depressive and anxiety symptom burden and with suicide risk (mediated by these symptoms). PRS-PheWAS linked the same score to 135 metabolic traits.
INTERPRETATION: The study leverages large, ancestrally diverse datasets and triangulates genetic, imaging and clinical data with several causal inference methods, strengthening internal validity. However, effect sizes for individual loci are modest and the PRS explains only a small fraction of variance in clinical outcomes; thus statistical significance does not yet translate into clinically actionable prediction. Population specificity (EAS-only discovery) limits immediate generalisability to European or other ancestries. The mediation findings are observational and cannot establish causality.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: At present, these results do not change bedside practice; they highlight potential mechanistic pathways (lipid/neurotransmitter biology, parietal-temporal cortex development) and risk domains (mood symptoms, suicidality, metabolic comorbidity) that may inform future stratified or preventative strategies rather than guide current treatment choices.

item.title: [7] Jail-based opioid treatment implementation, outcomes, and costs: lessons learned from the Massachusetts Justice Community Opioid Innovation Network (MassJCOIN).
item.description:
BACKGROUND: The study examines the implementation, outcomes, and costs of jail-based medications for opioid use disorder (MOUD) in Massachusetts, where a legislative mandate required pilot jails to offer all FDA-approved MOUDs, ensure continuity upon release, and facilitate community continuation. It is a Type 1 hybrid effectiveness-implementation study conducted within the Massachusetts Justice Community Opioid Innovation Network (MassJCOIN), focusing on incarcerated individuals with opioid use disorder.
